note: Reading glossary: structural words and formulas. Drafted and reviewed by Opus 5.5 (served-model checked); single words cross-checked against Jastrow via Sefaria where an entry exists. No sages names.

אמר: Introduces a statement by a named authority.
אלא: Rejects the previous suggestion and introduces a new one.
מאי: Asks for the meaning, reason or content of something.
הא: Points to a case or raises a contradiction. 'הא... הא' means 'this case... that case'.
והא: Introduces a challenge from a known source or fact.
דהא: Supports a point with a known fact.
אי: Opens a conditional, often one side of a dilemma.
ואי: Often presents the other horn of a dilemma.
דאי: Explains by showing the alternative would fail.
משום: Gives the reason or source of a ruling.
לאו: Can open a leading question ('is it not that...?'). It also denotes a negative commandment.
קא: Particle before a participle marking continuous or present action.
כתיב: Cites a verse, often to raise a difficulty.
וגו׳: Marks that a quoted verse continues beyond the cited words.
רחמנא: Refers to what the Torah states.
שמע: Appears in תא שמע ('come and hear') and שמע מינה ('learn from it').
תא: Appears in תא שמע, which introduces a source to resolve a question.
מינה: Appears in שמע מינה, 'conclude from it'.
הכא: Refers to the present case, often contrasted with התם.
התם: Refers to another case or source being compared.
טעמא: Asks for or states the reasoning behind a ruling.
לומר: Appears in תלמוד לומר, which introduces the verse that teaches the point.
תלמוד: Appears in תלמוד לומר: 'Scripture therefore says...'.
יכול: Introduces a mistaken inference that a verse then rules out.
סבר: States an authority's opinion or assumption.
קסבר: Explains a view by the principle behind it.
אימא: Proposes a reading or an alternative explanation.
ואיבעית: Appears in ואיבעית אימא, which introduces an alternative answer.
אמינא: Appears in הוה אמינא: the initial assumption before correction.
תימא: Appears in לא תימא ('do not say') and אי תימא ('if you say').
דתימא: Appears in מהו דתימא, which states the error a teaching prevents.
אילימא: Proposes an interpretation, usually to be rejected.
סלקא: Appears in סלקא דעתך: 'you might have thought'.
דעתך: Appears in סלקא דעתך, 'it would enter your mind'.
והתניא: Challenges a statement from a baraita.
תנו: Appears in תנו רבנן, which opens a baraita.
תנא: Introduces a baraita. Pointed תַּנָּא, it means a Tanna (tannaitic authority).
תני: Introduces a recited text or an emended reading.
קתני: Points to the exact wording of a source.
איתמר: Introduces an amoraic statement or dispute.
מיתיבי: Challenges an amora from a tannaitic source.
איתיביה: Challenges someone from a tannaitic source.
קשיא: States an objection, sometimes left unresolved.
איבעיא: Appears in איבעיא להו, which opens a question to be investigated.
בעי: Either poses a question or states a requirement.
מיבעי: Appears in מיבעי ליה, 'it is needed for (another teaching)'.
מיבעיא: Appears in לא מיבעיא: 'not only... but even'.
צריכא: Justifies why each of several teachings is needed.
קאמר: Appears in הכי קאמר: 'this is what it means'.
דאמרי: Appears in איכא דאמרי, which gives an alternative version.
אמרינן: States an accepted principle of reasoning.
והאמר: Challenges from a known amoraic statement.
דמי: Appears in היכי דמי: 'what is the case?'. Also in דמי ליה: 'is comparable'.
היכי: Appears in היכי דמי: 'what is the case?'.
למאן: Asks which view a statement follows.
כמאן: Asks which authority a ruling follows.
במאי: Appears in במאי עסקינן: 'what case are we dealing with?'.
מנא: Appears in מנא הני מילי, which asks for the source.
איני: Challenges a statement against another source.
שנא: Appears in מאי שנא: 'how does it differ?'.
שאני: Distinguishes a case to resolve a contradiction.
בשלמא: Concedes one side before raising a difficulty on the other.
לעולם: Reaffirms an original position with a new explanation.
דלמא: Suggests an alternative that weakens a proof.
דילמא: Suggests an alternative that weakens a proof.
היינו: that is; is the same as
Asks or states that two views or cases are identical.
שכן: Introduces a refutation of a קל וחומר by citing a distinguishing feature.
וחומר: Appears in קל וחומר, an a fortiori inference.
שוה: Appears in גזירה שוה, an inference from identical wording.
השתא: Introduces 'now that...' reasoning or a kal vachomer.
פשיטא: Questions why something self-evident needs stating.
מידי: In מידי הוא טעמא אלא: 'is the reason anything but...?'
לימא: Proposes a connection, often to be rejected.
עסקינן: Appears in הכא במאי עסקינן, which limits a source to a specific case.
אלמא: Draws a conclusion from a source.
מכלל: Infers an unstated position from what was said.
נפקא: Appears in מנא נפקא and נפקא מינה ('practical difference').
לרבות: Explains that a word extends the law.
למעוטי: Explains that a word limits the law.
מלמד: Appears in מלמד ש..., 'this teaches that...'.
בעלמא: Downgrades something to mere support, or refers to general cases.
דכולי: Appears in דכולי עלמא: 'according to all'.
אתא: Appears in למאי אתא: 'what does it come to teach?'.
מילי: Appears in הני מילי: 'this applies only when...'.
ההוא: Often introduces a story about an unnamed person.
חד: Appears in חד אמר... וחד אמר: 'one said... the other said'.
חדא: Appears in חדא ועוד: 'firstly, and moreover'.
קמא: Appears in תנא קמא, the first anonymous opinion.
לקמיה: Often in 'came before him' with a case or question.
בינייהו: Appears in מאי בינייהו: 'what is the practical difference?'.
קמיפלגי: Appears in במאי קמיפלגי: 'about what principle do they disagree?'.
גמ׳: Marks the start of the Gemara discussion.
מתני׳: Marks the start of the Mishnah text.
רישא: Refers to the opening clause of a source.
סיפא: Refers to the final clause of a source.
דרבנן: Marks a law as rabbinic, not biblical.
דאורייתא: Marks a law as biblical in force.
תנאי: The same spelling can mean 'Tannaim', as in תנאי היא ('it is a Tannaitic dispute').
והלא: but is it not so that
Introduces a rhetorical challenge from an accepted fact.
מודה: Marks that one side accepts the other's view on a point.
מודים: Marks agreement in a case despite a general dispute.
שפיר: Often in 'שפיר קאמר', approving a view or reading.
קרי: Usually 'reads/calls'; as a noun it means seminal emission.
חזי: Either 'see' or 'fit for use', depending on context.
מנת: portion; על מנת: on condition that
Introduces a stipulation attached to an act.
ואימא: Proposes an alternative interpretation to the one assumed.
לענין: Limits a statement to a specific area.
מהכא: Introduces a source for a derivation.
סברי: States the reasoning or opinion of a group.
נימא: Introduces a tentative proposal, often later rejected.
ההיא: Often refers back to a cited teaching or case.
כולי: In 'כולי עלמא', everyone agrees; in 'וכו'', etc.
ואלא: Introduces an alternative after rejecting a suggestion.
טעם: Asks or gives the rationale for a ruling.
וכמה: Asks for a measure or quantity.
מעתה: In 'אלא מעתה', draws an absurd consequence to refute.
אליבא: Frames a discussion within one sage's opinion.
ואידך: Asks how the other opinion handles the argument.
תנינא: Shows a statement is already taught in a Mishnah.
צריכה: Explains why seemingly redundant teachings are needed.
גופא: Returns to analyze a text quoted earlier in passing.
גזירה: Explains a rule as a precaution against a related violation.
אטו: Rhetorical rejection; or 'on account of' in decrees.
בעא: Introduces a question posed by a sage.
והתנן: but we learned in a Mishnah
Introduces a Mishnah that challenges the statement.
גמר: Indicates a derivation from another source.
מתוך: In 'מתוך ש...', since one thing applies, another follows.
מתיב: Introduces a source cited against a view.
משכחת: In 'משכחת לה', shows a case where the rule applies.
לאתויי: Explains what an extra word or clause adds.
להביא: Explains what an extra word or phrase comes to add.
לאפוקי: Explains what a word or clause comes to exclude.
אתיא: In 'אתיא X X', derived by gezera shava from a shared word.
למימרא: Infers an implication from a statement, often to question it.
תאמר: In 'ואם תאמר', introduces a possible objection.
מתני: Marks the Mishnah text; as a verb, 'teaches'.
לישנא: Introduces an alternate version of a tradition.
מכדי: Opens a premise leading to a question.
ניחא: Accepts one side before raising a difficulty on another.
הניחא: Concedes one view fits, then asks about the other.
ותניא: Cites a baraita, often as a challenge or support.
ממאי: from where; how do we know
Questions the basis of an assumption.
דמר: Refers to a cited sage's view.
לטעמיה: Shows a view follows the sage's known position.
דנין: Used for inferences from one case to another.
ודלמא: Rejects a proof by offering another reading.
איצטריך: Explains why a teaching or verse is needed.
תיבעי: Raises a question that arises from an analysis.
אשמעינן: Identifies the new point of a teaching.
וקתני: Points to wording in a source.
אמרן: In 'לא אמרן אלא', restricts a ruling to a case.
בעית: In 'אי בעית אימא', offers an alternative answer.
דומיא: Argues a case parallels another in the source.
אתמר: Introduces an Amoraic dispute or statement.
קיימא: In 'קיימא לן', it is established for us.
והיינו: Identifies two things as the same.
אמר ליה: Introduces a reply or objection in a dialogue between two speakers.
מאי טעמא: Asks for the reasoning or source behind a ruling.
תלמוד לומר: the verse teaches (lit. learning to say)
Introduces the verse that resolves an exegetical question.
קא משמע: Part of קא משמע לן: states the novel point a source teaches.
קמשמע לן: Short for קא משמע לן; the text may write it as one word, קמשמע לן. States the novel point being taught.
תא שמע: Brings a source as proof or as a resolution of a question.
על פי: Also completes אף על פי, 'even though'.
על גב: Usually part of אף על גב, 'even though'.
שמע מינה: Draws a conclusion; as a question it means 'can we conclude this?'
אמר לו: Introduces a reply in a Hebrew-language dialogue.
סלקא דעתך: Introduces a supposition that is then rejected.
אי הכי: Draws a difficulty from what was just said.
למאן דאמר: according to the one who says
Examines a question within one side of a dispute.
ברוך הוא: Ending of הקדוש ברוך הוא, referring to God.
לא קשיא: Resolves a contradiction, often by distinguishing two cases.
למה לי: Questions an apparently superfluous statement or verse.
אם כן: Draws a consequence, often a difficulty.
הכא נמי: Applies the same reasoning to the present case.
הכי נמי: Concedes a point ('yes, indeed'), or applies it similarly.
וחכמים אומרים: Introduces the majority view opposing an individual.
אמר קרא: Cites the verse that serves as the source.
הרי זה: States the legal status in a ruling.
הכי קאמר: Reinterprets a statement to remove a difficulty.
הני מילי: Limits a ruling to certain cases.
מאי לאו: Proposes a reading of a source as a proof, often then rejected.
או דלמא: Introduces the second side of a question.
או דילמא: Introduces the second side of a question.
היכי דמי: Asks for the precise circumstances of a ruling.
מיבעי ליה: Shows a verse is needed for another teaching. Can also mean 'he should'.
במאי עסקינן: Introduces a restriction of a source to a specific case.
הכא במאי: Opens הכא במאי עסקינן, limiting a source to a special case.
וכי תימא: Anticipates a possible answer and rejects it.
מתקיף לה: Introduces an objection by a later scholar.
אי אמרת: Tests a possibility by drawing its consequence.
אמר מר: Quotes a line of a source just cited, for analysis.
אמר לך: Shows how a disputant would defend his view.
אלא לאו: Rejects one reading and proposes the alternative as proof.
מהו דתימא: States the mistaken assumption a teaching comes to exclude.
לא שנו: they taught only (lit. did not teach)
Opens לא שנו אלא, limiting a mishnah to one case.
הוה אמינא: States what one would have assumed without the teaching.
איבעיא להו: Introduces an unresolved question for discussion.
לא צריכא: Introduces the specific case where a ruling is needed.
מאי שנא: Asks why two similar cases are treated differently.
ומאי שנא: Asks why two similar cases are treated differently.
דכולי עלמא: Marks a point accepted by all parties.
כולי עלמא: Marks a point agreed by all disputants.
ואמרי לה: Gives an alternate attribution or version.
איכא דאמרי: Introduces an alternate version of a discussion.
ואיכא דאמרי: Introduces an alternate version of a discussion.
ומר סבר: Presents the opposing side of a dispute.
מר סבר: Presents one side of a dispute.
איכא בינייהו: States the practical difference between two views.
מאי בינייהו: Asks for the practical difference between two views.
דברי הכל: Marks a point accepted by all parties.
מאי איכא: Often מאי איכא למימר, 'what can be said?'
הוא אומר: Introduces a verse or a further statement.
כי אתא: Introduces a teaching brought from another place.
מאי דכתיב: what is (meant by) what is written
Introduces an exposition of a verse.
סבר לה: States that a scholar follows a certain view.
אית ליה: States that a scholar accepts a principle.
לית ליה: he does not hold; he has not
States that a scholar rejects a principle.
דאמר קרא: Gives the verse that is the source.
מה להלן: Draws an analogy from another verse or case.
כתב רחמנא: Cites what the Torah explicitly states.
תניא נמי: Brings a baraita supporting a statement.
במה דברים: in what case are these words
Opens במה דברים אמורים, limiting a ruling.
דברים אמורים: Part of במה דברים אמורים, 'when does this apply?'
אלא מעתה: Pushes a proposed principle to an absurd conclusion.
עד כאן: Often 'so far' a view extends, e.g. עד כאן לא קאמר.
הוה ליה: Classifies a case under a category.
אין לי: In midrash: the verse alone teaches only this case.
אינו דין: Introduces a logical (often a fortiori) inference.
אפילו תימא: Shows a source fits even the view thought to conflict.
מה תלמוד: Opens מה תלמוד לומר, asking why a verse is needed.
לא שנא: States that two cases are treated alike.
ולא שנא: States that two cases are treated alike.
משכחת לה: Shows a case where a ruling can apply.
היכי משכחת: Asks for a possible scenario of a ruling.
בעא מיניה: Introduces a question posed to a teacher.
הרי אלו: States the legal status of several items.
חד אמר: Introduces one of two opposing views.
וחד אמר: Introduces the second of two opposing views.
אימא סיפא: Cites the end of a source to raise or resolve a difficulty.
שאני התם: Rejects a proof by distinguishing the cited case.
אמרת בשלמא: Concedes one view works, before challenging the other.
בשלמא למאן: Concedes the difficulty fits one view but not the other.
הניחא למאן: this works for the one (who says)
Concedes one view, then challenges the other.
כי פליגי: Defines the case in which the dispute exists.
תנא קמא: The anonymous first opinion in a mishnah or baraita.
אתא לקמיה: Introduces a case brought to a scholar.
מאן תנא: Asks which Tanna an anonymous source follows.
ומאן דאמר: Presents the other side of a dispute.
מי לא: Rhetorical question asserting something is so.
קא מיפלגי: Identifies the principle at the root of a dispute.
בהא קמיפלגי: Identifies the principle at the root of a dispute.
במאי קמיפלגי: Asks for the principle underlying a dispute.
מה לי: Argues two cases should be the same.
תניא כוותיה: a baraita was taught in accord with him
לא יצא: he has not fulfilled his obligation
מכל מקום: Holds a point true regardless of the preceding.
הכתוב מדבר: Identifies the case a verse refers to.
דאמרי תרוייהו: Cites a statement made jointly by two scholars.
מסייע ליה: Introduces a source supporting a statement.
הא כיצד: Introduces a harmonization of conflicting statements.
תנאי היא: it is a dispute of Tannaim
Shows an issue is already disputed among Tannaim.
מנא הני: Asks for the scriptural source of a ruling.
מנא לן: Asks for the source of a ruling.
מן התורה: Marks a law as biblical, not rabbinic.
אלא מאי: Challenges by asking what the alternative could be.
נפקא מינה: States the practical difference resulting from a distinction.
נפקא ליה: Gives a scholar's source for a law.
לרבות את: States what a word in a verse comes to add.
לטעמיה דאמר: follows his reasoning, for he said
Links a view to the scholar's known principle.
מי אמרינן: Asks whether a principle applies here.
כתיב הכא: First half of a gezera shava comparison.
וכתיב התם: Second half of a gezera shava comparison.
מאי איריא: Asks why a source chose this case.
זה הכלל: Introduces a general principle summarizing cases.
כשהוא אומר: Brings another verse to settle an exegesis.
גופא אמר: Returns to analyze a statement cited earlier.
לא קתני: Notes what a source omits, to draw an inference.
תיבעי לך: Says the question applies even under another view.
נמי תנינא: Shows a ruling is already in a mishnah.
ולא כלום: Declares an act or statement legally void.
ואי אשמעינן: and if it had taught us
Explains why multiple cases are needed.
לא נחלקו: Limits a dispute to a specific case.
לא מיבעיא: Opens a 'not only... but even' structure.
נאמר כאן: Begins a verbal analogy between verses.
מאי קאמר: Questions the coherence of a statement.
נמי מסתברא: Adds logical support for a view.
גזירה שמא: Explains a rabbinic decree preventing a possible violation.
על אחת: Opens על אחת כמה וכמה, an a fortiori conclusion.
קא משמע לן: States the new point that a source comes to teach.
הקדוש ברוך הוא: the Holy One, blessed be He
לא שנו אלא: they taught this only (in a case)
Restricts a Mishnah's ruling to a particular case.
לא קשיא הא: Resolves a contradiction by assigning each source to a different case.
הכא במאי עסקינן: here, what are we dealing with?
Introduces a narrowing of the case to resolve a difficulty.
סלקא דעתך אמינא: you might have thought, I would say
Presents the mistaken assumption that a source comes to exclude.
מאי איכא למימר: Presses a difficulty that seems to have no answer.
תניא נמי הכי: a baraita was also taught thus
Brings tannaitic support for a statement just made.
במה דברים אמורים: in what case were these words said?
Introduces a limitation of the preceding ruling.
מה תלמוד לומר: what does the verse come to teach?
Asks why a seemingly superfluous word or verse is needed.
אלא למאן דאמר: but according to the one who says
Raises a difficulty for the other side of a dispute.
לא קשיא כאן: Resolves a contradiction by distinguishing two cases.
עד כאן לא: Limits a sage's ruling to its case, denying extension.
ואי סלקא דעתך: Introduces a reductio against a supposition.
אין לי אלא: Midrash: the verse covers only this; what about others?
אלא אי אמרת: Shows the alternative view runs into difficulty.
לא כל שכן: is it not all the more so?
אי אמרת בשלמא: Shows one view works, before challenging the other.
כולי עלמא לא: Marks a point of consensus within a dispute.
לא דכולי עלמא: Rejects the proposed link of a dispute to another view.
מנין תלמוד לומר: Midrashic question and its scriptural source.
מנא הני מילי: Asks for the scriptural source of a law.
או אינו אלא: Midrash: proposes an alternative reading of a verse.
בשלמא למאן דאמר: granted, according to the one who says
Concedes one view, setting up a challenge to the other.
הניחא למאן דאמר: this works for the one who says
Concedes one view, then asks about the other.
מאי קא משמע: Asks what novelty a statement contains.
לא אמרן אלא: Restricts a previous statement to a specific case.
אי בעית אימא: Introduces the first of alternative answers.
היכי דמי אילימא: what is the case? If you say
Asks for the case, then rejects a first proposal.
לאו שמע מינה: may we not infer from it?
Rhetorically draws an inference from a source.
הני מילי היכא: Restricts a ruling to certain circumstances.
אמר אפילו תימא: he said: you may even say
Answers that even the problematic view fits.
היכי משכחת לה: Asks for a realistic case where the law applies.
הכי נמי מסתברא: Supports a view by logic or textual inference.
לית לן בה: we have no concern with it
Rules that something is permitted or unproblematic.
מנא אמינא לה: from where do I say it?
Speaker introduces proof for his own claim.
ההוא מיבעי ליה: he needs that for another teaching
Says a verse is used for another derivation.
מיבעי ליה לכדתניא: he needs it for what was taught
Says the verse is used for a baraita's teaching.
למאי נפקא מינה: Asks for the practical consequence of a distinction.
אנן נמי תנינא: we also learned it (in a Mishnah)
Shows a stated ruling is already in a Mishnah.
מאי עביד ליה: what does he do with it?
Asks how the other side interprets a source.
אי סלקא דעתך: Introduces a supposition to refute it.
לעולם אימא לך: Returns to the original position after a challenge.
לא נצרכה אלא: Identifies the case that justifies a statement.
לא נצרכא אלא: Identifies the case that justifies a statement.
דיקא נמי דקתני: it is precise too, since it teaches
Supports an interpretation from the Mishnah's wording.
מי דמי התם: Rejects an analogy between two cases.
לימא מסייע ליה: shall we say it supports him?
Proposes support for an Amora, often rejected.
תנאי היא דתניא: it is a tannaitic dispute, as taught
Shows that Tannaim already disputed the issue.
מה אני מקיים: Asks how the other view explains a verse.
כי האי תנא: Identifies which tanna a view follows.
קמיפלגי מר סבר: Explains the logic of each side of a dispute.
בהא קמיפלגי דמר: in this they disagree: one master…
Pinpoints the underlying point of dispute.
במאי קא מיפלגי: Asks for the underlying point of dispute.
ואי כתב רחמנא: and if the Torah had written
Explains why both verses are needed.
וצריכא דאי אשמעינן: it is necessary: had it taught us
Justifies why seemingly redundant statements are all needed.
מאי לאו בהא: Proposes that a dispute hinges on this point.
דאי לא תימא: for if you do not say so
Proves a point by showing the alternative is untenable.
הא לא קשיא: Dismisses one difficulty, often before raising another.
תא שמע דתניא: come and hear, as was taught
אין בו משום: Rules that a prohibition does not apply.
כמאן אזלא הא: according to whom does this go?
Asks which tanna's view a source follows.
אם אינו ענין: Midrash: superfluous verse is applied to another topic.
הא לאו הכי: Draws an inference from the converse.
אי הכי היינו: if so, that is the same as
Objects that two views are now identical.
היינו תנא קמא: that is the same as the first Tanna
Asks what the second opinion adds.
איכא למיפרך מה: Refutes an analogy or a fortiori.
מהו מי אמרינן: what is the law? Do we say
Presents an inquiry with its two sides.
שאני התם דאמר: there it is different, since (it) says
ראי זה כראי: (not) the aspect of this like that
Part of 'lo re'i zeh kire'i zeh': cases differ; derive from common feature.
מיחסרא והכי קתני: it is lacking, and teaches thus
Emends the Mishnah by supplying missing words.
כי תיבעי לך: Redirects an inquiry to the truly doubtful case.
לא תיבעי לך: Says one case is clear, unlike another.
מה הפרט מפורש: just as the particular is explicit
In כלל ופרט וכלל: extends the law to cases resembling the particular.
לא נחלקו אלא: Limits the scope of a dispute.
תני תנא קמיה: Introduces a baraita recited before an Amora.
אין שומעין לו: we do not listen to him
והא אנן תנן: Challenges a statement from a Mishnah.
כל מקום שנאמר: Introduces a general rule of scriptural usage.
אלא הכי קאמר: rather, this is what it says
Reinterprets a statement after a difficulty.
והלא דין הוא: is it not a logical inference?
Proposes a logical derivation, questioning a verse's need.
מאי איכא בין: Asks for the practical difference between views.
מחבירו עליו הראיה: claimant from another bears burden of proof
Part of 'המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה': burden of proof is on the claimant.
הא גופא קשיא: Points to an internal contradiction in a source.
למה הדבר דומה: to what is the matter comparable?
והלא כבר נאמר: but has it not already been said
Objects that a verse is redundant or contradicted.
אפילו למאן דאמר: even according to the one who says
אפילו תימא רבנן: you may even say (it follows) the Rabbis
Shows a source fits even the opposing view.
כי תניא ההיא: Restricts a contradicting baraita to another case.
מני: Asks which Tanna authored a source.
אידי: Appears in אידי ואידי: 'both this and that'.
הא מני: Identifies the author of an anonymous source.
אידי ואידי: Shows two clauses refer to the same case.
מי כתיב: Rhetorical challenge: the verse does not actually say what was claimed.
קא סלקא דעתך: Introduces an initial assumption that the Gemara will reject.
ש״מ: States a conclusion drawn from a source, or a proof that is accepted.
ורמינהו: Introduces a source that contradicts the one just cited.
הא קא משמע לן: this is what it teaches us
Identifies the novel point of a statement that seemed superfluous.
ומי: Opens a rhetorical challenge expecting 'no'. Can also mean 'and who'.
ותסברא: and do you really think so?
Rejects the assumption just made as untenable.
תינח: Concedes one case, then raises a difficulty with another case.
א״ל: Introduces a reply or statement addressed to another person.
וכו׳: Indicates that a quoted source continues beyond the words cited.
ה״ק: Reinterprets or clarifies the intended meaning of a statement.
מ״ט: Asks for the reasoning or source behind a ruling.
ת״ש: Introduces a source offered as proof or to resolve a question.
כ״ע: Signals that all disputing parties agree on this point.
ק״ו: Argument from a lenient case to a stricter one, or the reverse.
ג״ש: Hermeneutic linking two laws through an identical word in both verses.
